title: Ethics, Trust, and the Boring Hard Work
subtitle: Behavior compounds. Posters don't.

audioChapters.label: Opening — the values poster on the wall

blocks.md:
Almost every Indian company has a values poster on the wall. Almost none of those posters predict any behavior. Trust is built (or broken) by what leaders *do* in the small, awkward moments — not by what's typeset above the elevator.

This lesson is the boring hard work: post-mortems, explicit ladders, and the reason values get printed in the first place.

blocks.alt: A framed poster on a wall showing 'Integrity · Honesty · Boldness' next to a leader covering up a near-miss in a meeting. The trust meter drops below the poster.
blocks.caption: The poster says one thing; the behavior says the other. The team always reads the behavior.

blocks.title: Mental model: behavior compounds, posters don't
blocks.md:
Trust is a compounding asset. Every honest, slightly-uncomfortable disclosure adds. Every small cover-up subtracts. The compound rate is much faster than people expect.

A single public post-mortem of a real near-miss does more for org trust than 47 'lunch and learn' values sessions. It's costly to the leader; that's exactly why it works as a signal.

blocks.caption: Watch trust compound over time when behavior matches values — and crash when it doesn't.

hi-IN.title: All-hands ke speech vs. corridor ka behavior
hi-IN.md: Indian companies mein all-hands speeches mein 'integrity' word 14 baar aata hai. Corridor mein, manager ne junior ka kaam apna bola — team ne dekha. **Speech bhul jaata hai, corridor yaad rehta hai.** Posters $0 cost; behavior unbounded cost. Yahin se trust banta hai aur tootta hai.

en.title: Speeches vs corridors
en.md: All-hands speeches use the word 'integrity' often. Corridor behavior — what a manager does when they think no one is watching — is the actual signal. Teams remember corridors, not speeches.

blocks.md:
When something goes wrong on your watch, you have three options:

1. Cover it up. Hope no one notices. (Trust compound: -2% / week.)
2. Acknowledge privately, fix quietly. (Trust compound: 0%.)
3. **Public post-mortem.** What went wrong, what you missed, what changes structurally. (Trust compound: +3-7% per incident.)

The third option costs you in the short term and pays you in the long term. It's also the rarest. That's why it works as a signal.

blocks.alt: A timeline showing trust % over 12 months for three approaches: Cover-up (drops 24%), Quiet fix (flat), Public post-mortem (rises 47%). All three started from the same incident.
blocks.caption: Same incident, three responses, three trajectories. The cheap option in the moment is the expensive option over a year.

blocks.title: Translation moment: 'we shipped a feature that mishandled user data for 4 hours'

steps.label: Day 0 — the incident
steps.body: Feature shipped. Bug discovered. Some users affected. The clock starts.

steps.label: Hour 4 — internal triage
steps.body: Engineering rolls back. Damage assessed. The blame instinct kicks in.

steps.label: Hour 8 — choice point
steps.body: Cover up? Quiet fix? Public post-mortem? Most leaders default to option 2 because it 'feels balanced'. The team sees option 2 as option 1 in a smaller font.

steps.label: Day 1-2 — write the post-mortem
steps.body: What happened, why we missed it (without scapegoating), what changes structurally (eval, review process, incident playbook). Specific. No 'we will be more careful.'

steps.label: Day 3 — share publicly
steps.body: All-hands or written form. Acknowledge the harm to users. Walk through the fix. Take questions. The discomfort is the cost; the trust is the return.

blocks.prompt: What's the trust impact of a public post-mortem on a real incident, vs covering it up?

choices.label: Public post-mortem builds trust over time; cover-ups erode it slowly but compound to a much larger loss
choices.explain: Correct. The asymmetry is what most leaders underestimate. Discomfort is short; the compounding is long.

choices.label: They're roughly equivalent if no one notices the cover-up
choices.explain: Cover-ups are noticed eventually; the team always reads behavior. The 'no one notices' assumption is the trap.

choices.label: Public post-mortems destroy trust because they advertise weakness
choices.explain: Inverse of the truth. Pre-committed transparency builds trust; concealed weakness destroys it.

choices.label: The trust impact is symbolic; what matters is the technical fix
choices.explain: Technical fix matters but the trust impact is real and measurable. Both matter; trust compounds longer.

hi-IN.title: Indian context — 'log kya kahenge' ka counter
hi-IN.md: *"Public post-mortem mein log judge karenge"* — yes, they will. **Lekin woh log already judge kar rahe hain, sirf data ke saath ya bina.** Public post-mortem mein tu data control karta hai, gossip nahi. Indian corporate culture mein 'face-saving' ka cost trust se zyada hai.

en.title: Face-saving costs trust
en.md: The 'people will judge me' instinct is real. But people are already judging — they just don't have the data. A public post-mortem gives you control of the narrative; concealment gives them control via gossip.

blocks.md:
Most ethics fights at work are not 'is X right or wrong?'. They're *'who decides whether X is right or wrong, and how does that decision get made?'*

The **explicit ladder** is a written, before-the-incident document that says:
- These decisions are made by individual contributors.
- These by managers.
- These by directors.
- These by VPs.
- These by the CEO.
- These by the board.

When a hard call comes — and it will, especially in AI — everyone already knows whose call it is. Ambiguity is the trap; the ladder is the fix.

blocks.alt: A 6-rung ladder labeled IC, Manager, Director, VP, CEO, Board. At each rung, examples of decisions: 'IC: tool choice', 'Manager: project priority', 'Director: budget shifts', 'VP: org changes', 'CEO: strategic pivots', 'Board: existential bets'.
blocks.caption: Decisions get made; the ladder says by whom. Ambiguity is the source of nearly every escalation cycle.

intro: Right. Five real escalations from real Indian companies. ⚖️
Tell me **who's call** each one is — IC, Manager, Director, VP, CEO, or Board?
When the ladder is ambiguous, the cost is paid in weeks of escalation. Pick wisely.

scenarios.situation: Engineer wants to use Claude Sonnet 4.6 instead of GPT for a feature; cost diff +12%, quality diff +6%.
scenarios.explain: IC call. Tool choice within an existing capability budget is the IC's. Escalating wastes everyone's time.

scenarios.situation: Manager wants to reorganize her 8-person team into two pods of 4. Same heads, same budget.
scenarios.explain: Manager call. Same budget, same heads, structural change within their span. Loop the director for visibility, but it's the manager's call.

scenarios.situation: Director wants to lay off 30% of her org because AI automated their work; CEO and CFO not yet aware.
scenarios.explain: VP / CEO call. Layoffs of this size cross legal, financial, PR, and culture surfaces. Director should propose; VP/CEO decide.

scenarios.situation: CEO wants to pivot the company from B2B SaaS to a B2C AI consumer app; would change everything.
scenarios.explain: Board call. Strategic pivot of this magnitude requires board approval per the company's articles. CEO can propose; board decides.

scenarios.situation: Senior IC wants to publish a research paper that mentions a customer's name. Customer hasn't approved.
scenarios.explain: Director call. Crosses legal/customer surface; IC and manager don't have authority to commit the company externally. Director or VP signs off after legal review.

blocks.title: The classic trap: ambiguous decision rights
blocks.md:
Most 'ethics issues' at work are decision-rights issues in disguise.

A director makes a call that should have been a VP's; six months later it surfaces and the VP is angry. *"Why didn't you tell me?"* — the director didn't know they had to. The fix is not 'be more careful'; the fix is *write the ladder down before the next incident*.

A written ladder, reviewed annually, is one of the highest-trust documents an org can produce. Most don't have one. That's the gap.

blocks.prompt: Order these culture-building behaviors from highest to lowest long-run trust impact:

items.label: Public post-mortem of a real incident, with structural changes named
items.detail: Highest. Costly to the leader; rare; signals integrity decisively.

items.label: Written explicit ladder of decision rights, reviewed annually
items.detail: High. Removes ambiguity; prevents most 'ethics' fights before they start.

items.label: Quarterly all-hands speech on values
items.detail: Low. Mostly forgotten by the corridor.

items.label: Framed values poster on the wall

blocks.instruction: Pick one decision rights ambiguity that has caused friction on your team. Write the proposed ladder entry: who decides, who's consulted, who's informed (RACI is fine). Make it specific enough that the next time this comes up, no one has to escalate to find out.
blocks.expected:
Decision: 'Switching customer-facing AI feature from one model provider to another.'

- **Decides (R):** Director of Product (cost > ₹5L/month surfaces).
- **Approves (A):** VP Engineering (technical viability + risk).
- **Consulted (C):** Senior eng lead, legal (data residency), security (data flow).
- **Informed (I):** CFO, CMO, customer success lead.

Review cadence: every 6 months at the quarterly ops review. Stored at /docs/decision-ladder.md.

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO TRUE statements about org trust:

choices.label: Behavior compounds; values posters do not
choices.explain: Correct. Trust is a function of small, repeated, costly-to-fake behaviors.

choices.label: Pre-written decision ladders prevent most 'ethics' escalations
choices.explain: Correct. Most ethics issues at work are decision-rights issues in disguise.

choices.label: Public post-mortems destroy trust because they advertise weakness
choices.explain: Inverted. Concealment destroys trust; pre-committed transparency builds it.

choices.label: Quarterly values speeches are the highest-leverage culture move
choices.explain: Speeches are low-leverage; written ladders and public post-mortems compound far better.

hi-IN.title: Boring kaam — but sabse important
hi-IN.md: Yeh chapter ka theme: ethics ka kaam glamorous nahi hai. Post-mortem likhna, ladder draft karna, awkward conversations — sab thoda boring lagta hai. **Boring isliye kyunki ye actually compound karta hai.** Glamorous wala 'inspirational speech' usually nothing compounds.

en.title: Boring is the point
en.md: Ethics work is unglamorous: writing post-mortems, drafting ladders, sitting through awkward conversations. The unglamorous-ness is the point — it compounds in a way speeches don't.

points: Trust is a compounding asset built by small, costly-to-fake behaviors
Public post-mortems on real incidents are the highest-leverage trust-building move
Most 'ethics issues' are decision-rights issues in disguise; a written ladder fixes 80% of them
Values posters predict no behavior; behavior predicts itself
The unglamorous discipline (post-mortems, ladders, RACI) compounds; speeches don't

blocks.prompt: What's one decision rights ambiguity on your team right now that, if written down, would prevent the next escalation? Draft the entry today.
